assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the course and condition of a river system shaped the spatial distribution of early settlements.
assessment_items.question_text: The Sarasvatī River once supported major Harappan cities including Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala, Kalibangan, and Bhirrana along its course. Today the river flows only seasonally and is much reduced. What does the high density of Harappan sites along the now-seasonal river best tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: Harappan cities were built wherever the terrain was flat enough for construction, and the Sarasvatī corridor happened to be flat.

options.label: B
options.text: The river once flowed more strongly and reliably, providing the water and fertile soil conditions that made dense settlement possible in this corridor.

options.label: C
options.text: The Harappans chose this river specifically because it was already seasonal and easy to cross, making trade between cities simpler.

options.label: D
options.text: The Rig Veda's description of the river as a goddess caused communities to settle near it for religious reasons rather than practical ones.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Replaces the river-as-resource explanation with a terrain explanation — the chapter does not credit flat terrain as the driver of settlement along this corridor; students who select this have missed the water-and-soil logic.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Inverts the river's historical condition — a seasonal river would have been a weaker basis for settlement, not an easier crossing; students who select this misread the evidence of decline as a feature of the original river.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Presents religious reverence as the cause of settlement rather than as a cultural expression of an already-settled relationship with the river — this confuses correlation (the river is revered in texts) with causation.

assessment_items.chapter_section: The End or a New Beginning?
assessment_items.question_text: Around 2200 BCE, a global climatic change caused reduced rainfall across the region. The Sarasvatī River also dried up in its central basin. What was the direct effect of these two environmental changes on Harappan settlements?

options.label: A
options.text: Harappans expanded their trade to import more food, which led to larger cities rather than smaller ones.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced rainfall made agriculture more difficult, and the drying of the Sarasvatī led to the sudden abandonment of cities like Kalibangan and Banawali.

options.label: C
options.text: The Harappans moved their cities to higher ground to escape the effects of reduced rainfall and drought.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduced rainfall strengthened the drainage and reservoir systems because less water meant easier maintenance.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Applies a modern economic response (import substitution) to an ancient agricultural society — trade could not compensate for agricultural failure at the scale described; students who select this are importing modern assumptions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces highland relocation as a response — the chapter describes dispersal into small rural settlements, not movement to higher ground; students who select this confuse dispersal with migration.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misapplies a mechanical logic — less water does not make water infrastructure easier to maintain when the system was designed for abundant water; students who select this are reasoning in the wrong direction about infrastructure and climate.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the uneven geographical distribution of raw materials — carnelian in Gujarat, copper from outside the civilisation — drove the formation of long-distance trade networks.
assessment_items.question_text: Carnelian, a reddish semiprecious stone used to make the Harappans' most prized beads, is found mainly in Gujarat. Copper was likely imported from outside the civilisation. What does the geographical distribution of these two materials most directly explain about Harappan trade?

options.label: A
options.text: It explains why Gujarat became the political capital of the Harappan civilisation — control over carnelian gave it authority over other regions.

options.label: B
options.text: It explains why the Harappans needed long-distance trade: some essential or prized materials were only available in specific, often distant, locations.

options.label: C
options.text: It explains why the Harappans stopped trading after these deposits were exhausted — the trade network collapsed when carnelian and copper ran out.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains why Harappan craftspeople moved to Gujarat permanently to work with carnelian rather than transporting the stone to other cities.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Invents a political-authority claim that has no basis in the chapter — the chapter does not identify Gujarat as a capital or link carnelian control to political power; students who select this project modern resource-politics logic onto the ancient world.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces depletion as the explanation for trade collapse — the chapter attributes decline to climate change and river drying, not resource exhaustion; students who select this conflate the decline's actual causes with a plausible but unchapter-supported one.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Invents a craftsperson-relocation pattern — the chapter describes stone being transported and worked into beads by craftspeople with special drilling techniques, not mass relocation to source sites; this tests whether students can distinguish producing at the source from transporting and producing elsewhere.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how differential water infrastructure across Harappan cities reflects varying local resource conditions and engineering responses.
assessment_items.question_text: Mohenjo-daro had hundreds of brick-lined wells to supply water, while Dholavira built at least six large reservoirs cut into rock. What is the most likely reason these two cities used such different solutions?

options.label: A
options.text: Dholavira's rulers preferred stone structures as a symbol of status, while Mohenjo-daro's rulers preferred brick to match their city's building style.

options.label: B
options.text: The two cities had different local conditions — underground water availability, geology, and rainfall patterns — that made different engineering solutions appropriate.

options.label: C
options.text: Mohenjo-daro had a larger population than Dholavira, so it needed more water sources, which is why it built more wells rather than reservoirs.

options.label: D
options.text: Dholavira was built later than Mohenjo-daro, so its engineers had learned from Mohenjo-daro's mistakes and improved the design.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Attributes the engineering difference to elite status preference — the chapter gives no such claim; students who select this apply a social-prestige explanation where a resource-and-geology explanation is supported.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Uses population size as the explanatory variable — the chapter does not give comparative population data or use population as the explanation; students who select this supply a plausible but unsupported variable.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a temporal learning progression — the chapter does not establish which city was built first or frame Dholavira as an improvement on Mohenjo-daro; students who select this impose a modern design-iteration narrative onto the evidence.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify specific cultural practices and symbols from an ancient civilisation that have persisted into contemporary South Asian life.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter notes that several elements of Harappan cultural life can be recognised in South Asia today. Which of the following is the most accurate pairing of a Harappan cultural element with its surviving form?

options.label: A
options.text: The Harappan Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro → still used as a public bathing site by local communities in Pakistan today.

options.label: B
options.text: The terracotta figurine in the namaste pose → the namaste gesture still used as a common greeting across South Asia today.

options.label: C
options.text: The Dancing Girl figurine → a dance form still performed in Gujarat and Rajasthan that traces directly back to Harappan choreography.

options.label: D
options.text: The steatite seals → still used by South Asian merchants as commercial stamps in the same material and design.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Claims the Great Bath is still in active use — the chapter does not make this claim; the Bath's purpose is debated and it is an archaeological site, not a functioning facility; this tests whether students confuse surviving physical remains with surviving cultural practice.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Over-specifies the cultural continuity claim by asserting a direct choreographic lineage — the chapter identifies the figurine as suggesting dance was part of Harappan life, not that a specific traceable dance form survived; students who select this extend the claim beyond what the chapter supports.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Claims steatite seals are still used in the same form — the chapter does not make this claim; the seals' identification function is noted as analogous to modern trade marks, but the material and design did not persist; this tests whether students confuse functional analogy with actual survival.

assessment_items.chapter_section: The End or a New Beginning?
assessment_items.question_text: By 1900 BCE, Harappan cities had been abandoned, government had disappeared, and the population had dispersed into small villages. Yet the chapter says the civilisation's culture survived. Which of the following best supports the claim of cultural survival despite political collapse?

options.label: A
options.text: The Harappans rebuilt their cities in new locations along the Ganges river and continued their urban way of life unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Symbols such as the swastika, the namaste gesture, and artistic traditions continued to appear in later phases of Indian civilisation even after the cities were gone.

options.label: C
options.text: The Harappan script was eventually deciphered and its literature was preserved in later South Asian textual traditions.

options.label: D
options.text: Archaeological evidence shows that Harappan-style brickwork and city planning were adopted by Mesopotamian civilisations after the Harappan decline.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Claims a Ganges relocation and unchanged urban continuity — the chapter describes dispersal into rural settlements, not relocation of cities; this tests whether students have absorbed the nature of the dispersal.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Claims the script was deciphered — the chapter is explicit that the Harappan script remains undeciphered; students who select this confuse cultural survival (symbols, gestures) with textual transmission.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Claims Mesopotamian adoption of Harappan techniques — the chapter describes trade with Mesopotamia but not adoption of Harappan urban planning by Mesopotamian civilisations; students who select this over-extend the trade-connection evidence.
